chunks.title: Advice, Values and Hot Takes
chunks.text:
My advice for CS students, the skills I think matter in Pakistan right now, the values I care about, and a few hot takes.

Advice for a first-semester CS student: Don't rely entirely on university to make you a software engineer. The curriculum will teach you the fundamentals, but you have to teach yourself the industry skills. Build projects, even silly ones, and put them on GitHub from day one.

The skills that matter most for a CS student in Pakistan right now: 1. Problem-solving ability.
2. Knowing how to leverage AI tools without becoming dependent on them.
3. Strong communication skills. So many brilliant local developers fail to get international clients simply because they can't articulate their value in English.

The values that matter most to me: Integrity and continuous learning. In freelancing, being honest about your capabilities matters: missing a deadline while communicating early is always better than lying to a client. Continuous learning matters because the things we learn in tech go out of date incredibly fast.

Hot take on university degrees: University degrees are quickly becoming networking hubs rather than purely educational institutions.

Hot take on modern multiplayer games: Modern multiplayer games are too focused on competitive e-sports balancing. We lost the chaotic fun of casual server browsers.

Hot take on AI and software jobs: The things we learn become outdated very fast, so we need to keep up with tech. I also think there will be a really good business in building professional AI agents, the same agents that end up taking other people's jobs XD

chunks.title: My Freelancing Journey on Fiverr
chunks.text:
This is how I started freelancing, how I do my football edits and AI automation work, what my worst client taught me, and how I price my gigs.

Getting started on Fiverr: I started on Fiverr during my 2nd semester. Honestly, I was broke and wanted to upgrade my PC. It took about two agonising months of refreshing the app before I landed my first order, which was for $10. Since then I have grown into a Level 1 Seller with over 100 clients and 100+ positive reviews, and crossing my first $1,000 earned on Fiverr is one of the achievements I'm proudest of.

My football video editing workflow: First, I scour Twitter or YouTube for 4K broadcast clips or fan-cams. I pull them into Filmora and colour correct them, usually adding contrast and saturation to make the pitch pop. Then I spend the bulk of the time cutting the clips so they sync perfectly with the beat of the background track. A good 60-second edit takes me roughly 2 to 3 hours.

AI automation orders: On the AI side I get a lot of requests for RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) chatbots. For example, I recently built a system for an e-commerce client using LangChain and Pinecone. The bot ingests the client's massive product catalogue and handles customer support queries, recommending products based on natural-language prompts. Other work in this area uses n8n and LangGraph for automated workflows.

My worst client experience: I once took a fixed-price order from a client who completely ignored the initial scope. They demanded five major architecture revisions for a $50 app and threatened a bad review if I didn't comply.

What I learned: draw strict boundaries, document every requirement before starting, and never undersell complex work just to get a gig.

How I price my gigs: I currently use value-based pricing rather than charging by the hour. I get paid mainly through Payoneer, although their fees and deductions are really high.

Tips for starting on Fiverr in Pakistan: My advice for beginners in Pakistan: don't race to the bottom with pricing. Optimise your gig thumbnails. Stay online during US and EU hours at the start. And over-deliver massively on your first three orders to secure 5-star reviews. After that, the algorithm takes over.

Honesty with clients: Being honest about what you can do matters more than anything. If you are going to miss a deadline, communicating it early is always better than lying to a client.

chunks.title: How I Work, Study and Vibe Code
chunks.text:
This is how my normal days look, how I use AI tools when I code, how I study and learn, and how I deal with deadlines.

My normal routine: Mornings are usually spent at university attending lectures. When I get back I rest a bit. Late afternoons and evenings are for freelancing work and coding my personal projects. Late nights, after 11 PM, are strictly reserved for gaming with friends or watching football.

My vibe coding process and AI tools: Cursor is my primary IDE because of its inline AI capabilities. Claude is my go-to for complex architecture decisions and for debugging tough logic errors. I use ChatGPT mostly for brainstorming and for writing first drafts of documentation. For local experiments I also run open-source models through LM Studio and Ollama.

What I never let the AI do: I never let AI design the core database schema or write security logic without manual oversight. In my experience that always leads to technical debt. AI is great for speed and boilerplate, but the foundations and anything security-related get my own eyes on every line.

How I study for exams: For university exams I am, honestly, a chronic last-minute hyper-focuser. I compile past papers and my notes, and then I study intensely in the few days before the exam.

How I learn a new technology: For learning new tech I skip the tutorials and immediately try to build a micro-project with it. Breaking things and fixing them teaches me faster than watching someone else code.

chunks.title: Project Retrospective: The FocusSpace Pivot
chunks.text:
## Initial Concept: A Minimalist Student Dashboard
During my Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) coursework at UMT Sialkot, my usual team of classmates and I embarked on a project we called FocusSpace. The original vision was to build a highly minimalist student dashboard. We wanted to apply core HCI principles to reduce cognitive load, strictly limiting the number of UI elements on the screen to help students track their academic progress without feeling overwhelmed. We spent weeks mapping out user flows, designing wireframes, and ensuring the color palette and typography met accessibility standards.

## The 11th-Hour Pivot
Just one day before our final academic presentation, we realized the minimalist dashboard, while visually pleasing, lacked the technical depth required to truly stand out. In a massive, sudden shift, we pivoted the entire architecture. We abandoned the basic student dashboard concept and transformed FocusSpace into an AI-assisted website UI checker.

## The Challenge and Execution
This was not necessarily the hardest raw coding I have ever done, but it was incredibly challenging due to the intense thought process required to execute a pivot that late in the game. We had to figure out how to integrate an AI layer that could actively analyze a given web interface and provide real-time heuristic feedback based on the exact HCI principles we had been studying.

We mapped specific UI heuristics—like visibility of system status, error prevention, and aesthetic minimalism—into actionable prompts for the AI. The system would then parse UI elements and flag areas where a website violated these rules. The intense time crunch meant we had no room for error. We pulled a late-night session (fueled by Mr. Foodie burgers) to stitch the frontend interface to the backend logic.

## The Philosophy of Steam Profiles and Digital Aesthetics
When it comes to digital identity, I believe your Steam profile is a blank canvas. I spend a lot of time customizing digital Steam profiles, but I have a strong opinion here: I couldn't care less about crafted badges or game achievements. The true art lies in bespoke vector artwork, perfectly looped animated showcases, and tailored backgrounds. I use Adobe Illustrator for vector tracing and Photoshop for bringing AI-generated concepts to life.

Beyond static graphics, I genuinely enjoy the rhythm of video editing. Splicing together short-form digital video content—especially high-energy European football highlights—is one of my favorite creative outlets.

## Gaming Setup and Preferences
I am a late-night gamer at heart. My primary competitive arenas are Counter-Strike 2 and Team Fortress 2. I have a very specific take on optimal gaming performance: visual clarity and framerate trump graphical fidelity every time. That is why I strictly play CS2 on a 4:3 stretched resolution at 1440x1080. When paired with a 200 Hz display, the absolute smoothness gives a distinct mechanical advantage. I also recently added EA Sports FC 26 to my rotation to scratch the football itch virtually.

## Entertainment: Anime, Music, and Football
My taste in media is pretty focused. For anime, I appreciate the absolute classics and modern heavy hitters. *Great Teacher Onizuka* is top-tier because Eikichi Onizuka's character dynamic is unmatched, and I closely follow *Jujutsu Kaisen*, specifically for the raw intensity of Ryomen Sukuna.

chunks.title: Projects Deep Dive: Nemesis, Zenith, ERPify, the Store POS and the Campus Network
chunks.text:
This document goes deeper into the projects listed on my CV: what problem each one solves, how it works, what it is built with, what was hard, and where it stands right now.

Nemesis: my automated penetration testing tool: The problem Nemesis solves is simple: manual reconnaissance and the first round of vulnerability scanning are tedious and time-consuming for security researchers. Every engagement starts with the same boilerplate phase, so I built Nemesis to automate it.

How it works: you give Nemesis a target IP address or domain. It automatically runs layered nmap scans, starting with fast host discovery and moving step by step into deep service enumeration. It then parses the scan output and cross-references the open ports and detected services against known CVE databases, so it can highlight the immediate attack vectors instead of leaving you with a wall of raw scan results.

The stack: Nemesis is built heavily in Python. It uses standard libraries such as subprocess to run nmap, and custom parsing logic for nmap's XML output. I also use networking libraries like scapy for custom packet crafting.

The hardest part: reliably parsing raw nmap XML output and correlating it with external vulnerability databases without throwing false positives. The logic for handling edge cases, for example when ports drop packets, was honestly a headache.

Status: Nemesis works today as a command-line (CLI) tool. Next I want to add a clean web-based GUI, probably React on the front end with FastAPI on the back end, plus automated reporting that exports findings as a PDF.

chunks.title: Projects Deep Dive: Nemesis, Zenith, ERPify, the Store POS and the Campus Network
chunks.text:
Status: Nemesis works today as a command-line (CLI) tool. Next I want to add a clean web-based GUI, probably React on the front end with FastAPI on the back end, plus automated reporting that exports findings as a PDF.

Zenith: the habit RPG app: Zenith turns daily life into an RPG. You create a character and set habits, for example "Drink Water" or "Study for 2 hours". Completing a habit gives you XP. As you collect XP you level up, unlock classes (like Scholar for study habits or Warrior for fitness habits) and earn virtual gear. That is the "character evolution" idea: your character grows as you actually stick to your habits.

The screens: the Dashboard shows your character sprite with health and mana bars; the Quest Log holds your daily habits and to-dos; there is a Skill Tree; and there is a Shop where you spend the gold you earn on rewards.

Status: Zenith is a working prototype built in React Native. It runs on my phone, but I still need to polish the backend database before a public app store release.

ERPify: an ERP built for Pakistani SMEs: The problem: most Pakistani small and medium enterprises (SMEs) still run on old paper ledgers or on cracked, outdated software that does not understand the local context. ERPify handles invoices, inventory and GST/FBR tax compliance natively, and, importantly, it offers an Urdu interface so local shop staff can actually use it.

chunks.title: Projects Deep Dive: Nemesis, Zenith, ERPify, the Store POS and the Campus Network
chunks.text:
The AI part: I integrated a predictive model that analyses past sales data and alerts the owner before they run out of fast-moving stock. It adjusts for seasonal spikes, like the rush before Eid.

The stack is Next.js and PostgreSQL, designed as a multi-tenant SaaS ERP and POS platform.

Status: the MVP is deployed locally with a couple of beta testers. I am still iterating on the FBR tax reporting modules.

Ahmad Sanitary Store POS: Background: before I built this, my family's store, Ahmad Sanitary Store in Gujranwala, used completely manual paper ledgers (khata) for everything. Finding an old bill was a nightmare.

Features: a quick billing interface, automatic stock deduction when something is sold, low-stock alerts, and daily and monthly profit reports. It is a desktop app built with Electron, React, Tailwind CSS and SQLite.

Status: yes, it is used every day at the store, and it has become critical to how the store operates.

What I learned: real-world users do unpredictable things. Building this taught me how to handle extreme edge cases, how to design an intuitive UI that needs no training, and why regular local database backups matter so much.

Campus Area Network (CAN) simulation in Cisco Packet Tracer: What I built: a simulated campus network spanning five separate buildings: Admin, the CS Department, Engineering, the Library and the Hostels.

Campus Area Network (CAN) simulation in Cisco Packet Tracer: What I built: a simulated campus network spanning five separate buildings: Admin, the CS Department, Engineering, the Library and the Hostels.

The details: I implemented inter-VLAN routing so that departments are isolated from each other but can still communicate through specific gateways. I used OSPF as the primary routing protocol. I also set up DHCP, DNS and basic ACLs (Access Control Lists) for security.

Environment: the whole network was built and tested in Cisco Packet Tracer, not on real hardware.

chunks.title: The Vibe Coding Hackathon at UMT: How We Took 3rd Place
chunks.text:
The Vibe Coding Hackathon at the University of Management and Technology (UMT) is the competition behind the "3rd Position" award on my CV. Here is the full story.

The theme and the team: The theme was "AI for Local Solutions". I competed in a team of three. The idea was to build something with AI that solves a real problem here in Pakistan, not just a flashy tech demo.

What we built: We built an AI-driven disaster response coordinator. The app ingested social media reports and SMS messages, used them to map out flood-affected areas, and then optimised rescue routes to reach those areas. Floods are a real and recurring problem in Pakistan, so the use case felt very close to home.

Tools and time: We had exactly 24 hours. We relied heavily on Cursor for rapid boilerplate generation, so we could get the skeleton of the app up fast, and on Claude for debugging complex logic and for the mapping integrations. That split, Cursor for speed and Claude for the hard reasoning, is basically how I vibe code in general.

What went wrong: Midway through the night we hit nasty API rate limits. They broke our demo for about three hours, and honestly there was a lot of panic in that stretch. When your live demo stops working in the middle of a 24-hour hackathon, every minute feels long.

chunks.title: The Vibe Coding Hackathon at UMT: How We Took 3rd Place
chunks.text:
Tools and time: We had exactly 24 hours. We relied heavily on Cursor for rapid boilerplate generation, so we could get the skeleton of the app up fast, and on Claude for debugging complex logic and for the mapping integrations. That split, Cursor for speed and Claude for the hard reasoning, is basically how I vibe code in general.

What went wrong: Midway through the night we hit nasty API rate limits. They broke our demo for about three hours, and honestly there was a lot of panic in that stretch. When your live demo stops working in the middle of a 24-hour hackathon, every minute feels long.

What went right: Our pitch was incredibly solid. We focused on the UI and on the real-world applicability of the app in Pakistan. The judges loved that it wasn't just a tech demo but a product that addressed a real local problem.

The result and why it matters to me: We took 3rd position overall, and we did it against senior teams. Placing 3rd at the UMT hackathon is one of the two achievements I'm proudest of so far (the other is crossing my first $1,000 earned on Fiverr). Both proved to me that my skills have real-world value. The hackathon also taught me that a clear pitch about a real problem can matter as much as the code, and that you should always plan for third-party APIs failing at the worst possible moment.
